title: Galileo: Sidereus nuncius (1610), Il Saggiatore (1623), the Dialogo (1632), the Discorsi (1638) and the Lettera a Cristina di Lorena (1615, printed 1636)

license.payload: Per item, recorded in origin.items. Galileo Galilei died in 1642; the printings of 1610, 1623, 1632, 1636 and 1638 are in the public domain everywhere. The Internet Archive copies carry these statements: Sidereus nuncius (Smithsonian Libraries) 'Not in copyright'; Il Saggiatore, the Discorsi and the Nov-antiqua (University of Toronto, Fisher Library), and the Dialogo (Smithsonian Libraries), no rights statement. The transcriptions are from Antonio Favaro's Edizione Nazionale, Le opere di Galileo Galilei (Firenze: Barbèra, 1890–1909), volumes III, V, VI, VII and VIII (1892–1898), public domain in the United States (published before 1931) and Favaro's own term run (died 1922); the Wikisource pages are CC BY-SA 4.0 for the site's contributions, redistributed under the same licence.
license.record: CC-BY-4.0 applies to this seat record only.

normalization: Originals as fetched under original/: Internet Archive scans with their OCR layers, and the Wikisource HTML as served with its revision ids. text/<slug>.ocr.txt is the Archive's OCR with line endings normalized; text/<slug>.txt is the Wikisource parser output reduced by code, a work of several pages joined under '=== <title> ===' headings. Favaro's page markers ('[p. 224 modifica]') and footnote numbers ('[1]') are kept as Wikisource serves them. No text was corrected by hand. The seventeenth-century OCR reads long s as f; the loci in the OCR layers are phrases it read correctly, and the canonical sentences are verified in the Favaro layers. Some Latin passages of the Favaro Discorsi on Wikisource are themselves uncorrected OCR (the page is marked 'incompleto'), kept as served.
units: one text file per work and witness: each work's first printing (OCR) and Favaro's text (Wikisource)

scope: Held: the five works the ruling names, each in its first printing (scan and OCR layer) and in Favaro's Edizione Nazionale as transcribed on Wikisource. The Lettera a Cristina di Lorena, written in 1615, circulated in manuscript and was first printed at Strasbourg in 1636 as the Nov-antiqua, with a Latin version: that printing is the witness. Not held: the other works on the Archive (Istoria e dimostrazioni intorno alle macchie solari, 1613; Discorso intorno alle cose che stanno in su l'acqua, 1612; Le operazioni del compasso, 1606; the Latin Systema cosmicum, 1635); the McGill copy of the Dialogo (391 MB) and the Opere of 1744, both found; the Appendix of the Discorsi in Favaro's text. Liber Liber holds Galileo's texts only as zipped RTF, which the seat builder does not read; Wikisource was used.
why_seated: Galileo's books carry the turn from the telescope's first sight of the Moon's mountains and Jupiter's moons, through the claim that the book of nature is written in mathematics, to the dialogue that was condemned and the two new sciences written after the condemnation. The letter to the Grand Duchess sets out how Scripture and nature are to be read beside each other. Each work is held at its first printing beside a clean text, so that every famous sentence has an address in both.
ruling: Lee Sharks, 2026-10-30: "and then an ea-corpora seating... Einstein, Gödel, Tesla, Copernicus, Galileo, classical Arabic mathematicians... what is in the public domain, and what else? and just to be perverse lets seat the promised Klee notebooks with them"; to the proposed set: "yes, thats a good set".
